entry.title: My Learnings from Learning Reinforcement Learning (WIP)

link.title: My Learnings from Learning Reinforcement Learning (WIP)

entry.content:
Disillisionment

My journey with reinforcement learning has been full of disillusionments. While it is undoubtedly a difficult subject, the way it is taught in most schools makes it even harder than it needs to be. I hope to get straight to the heart of the matter in this blog post.

Pedagogy is Overrated

For one thing, I don’t think it is useful to teach ideas in the sequence in which they were discovered/invented. We’ve figured a lot of things out over the years, and it probably makes the most sense to go straight to the stuff that works.

Everything is a Bag of Tricks

Also, we should be honest with students about the fact that none of what we do in RL has a very strong theoretical grounding - at the end of the day, things proceed largely through trial and error. This is more art than science. Other than a high-level mathematical framework, most of the mathematics we introduce is, in my opinion, simply unneccessary. With that said, I’ll quickly go over the high-level framework here, before proceeding to my learnings.

If you go through the papers for landmark algorithms like PPO, you will very quickly find a paragraph/section buried somewhere in the paper that is just an ugly mess of tricks (and hyperparameter values). Calling these ‘algorithms’ and naming them is unhelpful, in my opnion. What really matters is the combination of tricks that worked well in tandem. I believe we should be teaching students individual tricks, and then present the algorithms as particular instances where collections of tricks have worked well.

What really needs to be learned is how to develop an intuition for which tricks work well together.

High-Level Mathematical Framework

The overall paradigm of RL is actually quite simple. You have an agent, you have an environment. The state of the environment changes when the agent interacts with it. However, if the agent interacts with the environment correctly, it can also get rewards! And that’s the thing the agent is trained to maximize. Examples - game playing, robotics manipulation tasks.

At the end of the day, all the shenanigans you do in RL are towards one goal and one goal only - learning a policy. That is, a mapping from state to action. If the agent learns a good policy, it will be able to get high rewards.

Note how the policy only needs to know the current state to decide the next action; this is where a computer/robot would differentiate itself from a human - the computer/robot looks at every state with fresh eyes, it is not psychologically affected by past bad moves. It only sees the truth - what moves lead to bad results and what moves lead to good ones.

What makes RL RL?

The fact that you start with no data, and the only way to collect it is to interact with the environment. This is the real crux of what sets RL apart from other paradigms of ML (like supervised and unsupervised learning). Whatever policy you are trying to train is the same policy you will collect data with. This can create a viscious feedback loop where collecting data with a bad policy leads to bad training data, which the agent then never learns from.

This is why so much time is spent in getting agents to explore their environment. Every well-known and practically useful RL algorithm today achieves this by introducing randomization into the actions predicted by its policy. That is, instead of outputting one action given a state, we have the policy output a distribution over the action space (introduce notation). Then, we can choose to sample from the distribution with high noise (to encourage exploration) or with low noise (to encourage exploitation). (Explain with examples; robot arm and game playing)

Distirbutional NNs

Training neural networks that output distributions is tricky, because sampling isn’t really a differentiable operation.

The Unneccessary Dichotomy of On-Policy and Off-Policy Algorithms

I have always found this to be an absurd distinction. In fact, is isn’t really a distinction. It is a continnum. You can choose to use a lot of old data (then you are off-policy). Or you can choose to use very little old data (the you are on-policy).

Granted, some methods lend themselves more naturally to one side of the spectrum than the other (for example, PPO is often classified a on-policy because it isn’t able to make good use of old data). But that is just a design choice that you make when crafting your code. It isn’t some fundamental distinction in the space of RL algorithms, and should not be presented as such. In fact, I would say this distinction should not be taught at all. Maybe just as an afternote saying “the research community like to classify RL method into two categories…”.

You can Optimize Anything

RL taught me a completely new way to think about deep learning. The parameters of a model need not be trained through a loss function (which is calculated with ground truth values). You could train it maximize/minimize any quantity that it outputs!

DDPG does exactly this. DDPG is what is called an actor-critic algorithm. This is just an umbrella term for an approach that has worked well for us. As usual, we try to train a policy (a.k.a, the ‘actor’). But we also train something called a value function (‘critic’). This value function takes in a state, and outputs the expected reward from that state. (Example with game playing). In DDPG, we do something really clever where we take a (state, action) pair from the replay buffer, pass it to the environment to see the next_state, and then pass it through the valu function to see the value of the next_state. The actor is then trained to maximize the value of the next_state (no loss function or ground truth comparison involved)!

entry.title: Create a Zero-Downtime Deployment of Your Machine Learning API

link.title: Create a Zero-Downtime Deployment of Your Machine Learning API

entry.content:
Swap out old models for new ones whenever you want without skipping a beat

One of the things that make Machine Learning APIs unique is that the underlying models need to constantly be retrained as new data comes in. This leads to frequent re-deployments, and as a consequence, frequent downtime.

In this article, I’ll be walking you through a solution that gets around this problem. The following GIF shows that solution in action. On the left is the API server that is running the (re-)deployment script. On the right is the client that is constantly pinging that API:

The API never returns an error even though the deployment script is running live on the server!

The code for this can be found on my GitHub. It is actually part of a template project that I am developing. More on that soon.

Blue-Green Deployments

The solution I have come up with is inspired by a technique called blue-green deployments.

The basic idea is simple: You spin up the container with your new model and wait until it’s ready. Then, your load balancer diverts traffic from the old deployment (blue in this animation) to the new deployment (green).

The rest of this article will explain how this is achieved, including the technologies used and the relevant code from the template project.

The Load Balancer — Traefik Proxy

Most people automatically use Nginx for load balancing, but the free Nginx load balancer is not able to dynamically detect changes in downstream servers. This is a problem for us because it makes the last step of the blue-green deployment strategy impossible.

That’s why we’ll be working with an alternative called Traefik Proxy.

Basic abstractions

Before understanding how Traefik solves our problems, we need to familiarize ourselves with its underlying abstractions.

This paragraph and the subsequent diagram (both taken directly from the Traefik Proxy documentation) give a nice starting point:

“When you start Traefik, you define entrypoints (in their most basic forms, they are port numbers). Then, connected to these entrypoints, routers analyze the incoming requests to see if they match a set of rules. If they do, the router might transform the request using pieces of middleware before forwarding them to your services.”

The diagram above can conceptually be further divided into two parts, each of which is configured separately.

Entry points are a part of the static configuration, while the routers and services are defined in the dynamic configuration. This means that you can add and remove routers and services on the fly, and Traefik will make sure that traffic always flows appropriately.

In terms of blue-green deployments, this means that we can bring up the green containers and bring down the blue containers without having to re-initialize Traefik. Since the downstream containers are part of the dynamic configuration, Traefik will automatically register those changes for us.

Let’s understand how this is achieved step by step.

Static configuration

The Traefik load balancer is brought up in a container of its own. This is the docker-compose service that describes how to create that container:

The entries under the command key constitute the static configuration. These come into effect when Traefik is brought up for the first time and can’t be changed later.

The complete list of possible static configurations can be found in the docs. If you go through the list, you’ll notice that there are no configuration options for routers or services. This is because those are dynamic components.

If you go down even further, you’ll start seeing configs for something called providers.

Providers and dynamic configuration

Providers are what make dynamic configuration possible in Traefik. The documentation elaborates on providers under the Configuration Discovery heading:

“Providers are existing infrastructure components, whether orchestrators, container engines, cloud providers, or key-value stores. The idea is that Traefik will query the providers’ API in order to find relevant information about routing, and each time Traefik detects a change, it dynamically updates the routes.”

In our case, the provider is the Docker daemon (if you go back up to the static configuration, you’ll find the entry providers.docker=True). Traefik communicates with the Docker daemon to gather information about active Docker containers.

So how do we translate between Docker containers and Traefik concepts like routers and services? Well, as a starting point, we have this guarantee from the documentation:

“Traefik creates, for each container, a corresponding service and router.”

To specify the configurations for that service and router, we use Docker container labels. Take a look at the service definition from the docker-compose.yml file:

The dynamic configurations are all provided under the labels key. Traefik uses them to dynamically create routers and services. The full list of dynamic configuration options can be viewed in the docs.

Dynamic configuration details (can be skipped): loadbalancer

You’ll notice that all of the dynamic configuration keys have loadbalancer in them. This is because it is possible to deploy many replicas of a single container (using the --scale option of the docker-compose up command). So, Traefik automatically configures the service corresponding to a container (or a set of replicas) as a load balancer.

Dynamic configuration details (can be skipped): healthcheck

Each container takes some time to prepare itself and get its API ready. To avoid sending requests to a container that isn’t ready yet, Traefik allows you to configure health checks. From the documentation:

“Traefik will consider your servers healthy as long as they return status codes between 2XX and 3XX to the health check requests.”

I’ve added a health check endpoint to the API at the end of theapp.py file:

Since it is the last endpoint defined in the file, we can be sure that if the /health endpoint is responding, all other endpoints and resources have been initialized successfully.

A Walkthrough of the Deploy Script

With that background, let’s go through the deploy script line by line and understand the entire process.

Initial setup

First, the setup:

I’ve designed the deployment so that all the containers are deployed on a single Docker network, deployed-containers. If we are deploying for the first time, a number of resources get initialized:

  1. First, the Docker network (deployed-containers).
  2. Then the reverse proxy (Traefik). This is done in the line docker-compose up -d reverse-proxy. This will load the static configuration shown earlier and set up Traefik to monitor changes from the Docker daemon.
  3. Finally, we need to initialize a file called .colors that keeps track of the color of the current/next deployment. I’m borrowing the idea of a colored deployment from blue-green deployments. This is an example of what the .colors file would look like at the beginning of the deployment that we will be running through:
export DEPLOYED_COLOR="blue"
export IDLE_COLOR="green"

Bringing up new (green) containers

In the beginning, things will be in this state:

We will begin by bringing up the green deployments:

There are two things to notice here:

  1. The — scale model=$REPLICAS. It tells docker-compose to build $REPLICAS replicas of the “green” deployment.
  2. The — p $IDLE_COLOR. It is used to specify a project namespace to docker-compose. This is important for isolating the green and blue deployments from each other.

That will bring us to this point:

Once the green deployments are ready (i.e. once the health checks are passing), Traefik will start sending traffic to those green deployments as well. Then we’ll be in this state:

Bringing down old (blue) containers

The next step is to bring down the blue containers. We have to do this manually, but only after the green containers are ready. Unfortunately, there’s no way to ping the health endpoints of the green or blue containers individually from outside of Traefik.

To get around this, I created a /deployment_color endpoint in the API. Using it, we can ping the Traefik load balancer and determine the color of the container that responded. As soon as we get a green response, we will know that the green containers are up and we can proceed to bring down the blue containers:

Remember how we isolated the blue and green containers into separate namespaces using the -p flag of docker-compose? That now allows us to bring down the blue containers without affecting the newly deployed green containers. Here’s a demonstration of the process on my local machine:

So after bringing down the blue containers, we will have arrived at our desired final state:

Cleanup

The only thing left to do now is to reset the values in the .colors file:

And to clean up any dangling resources:

Final Demonstration

Here’s a final demonstration of the re-deployment process run on a Linux server I rented from Digital Ocean:

And that’s zero-downtime deployment for you! Thanks for reading.

Resources

  • https://github.com/RishabhMalviya/ml-deployment-template
  • https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/routing/overview/
  • https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/reference/static-configuration/cli/
  • https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/reference/dynamic-configuration/docker/
  • https://github.com/RishabhMalviya/ml-deployment-template/blob/master/deploy.sh

entry.title: Why Kotlin has Mutable Collections
entry.content:
The reasons are deeper than you think.

Everything in Kotlin is slick and elegant— you never have to write unnecessary code, and the primitive language constructs just work. But the dichotomy between mutable collections and immutable collections feels like something that can be avoided. The fact that it’s such an integral part of the language must point to something deeper.

The simple, one-line explanation is this:

Mutable and immutable collections individually expose useful features that can’t co-exist in a single interface. Mutable collections are mutable, while immutable collections are covariant.

If that doesn’t make sense to you, don’t worry. The rest of this article was written to explain it to you!

Type Hierarchy

We need to establish some important things about the type of hierarchy before moving on.

Assign-ability

Consider the following variable:

Although the variable is declared with type Shape, you can actually store an object of type Rectangle in it. That’s because Rectangle is a subtype of Shape, so it will have at least all of the properties/fields/methods of Shape implemented.

Therefore, this is valid:

Which brings us to the first important point you need to remember:

When assigning an object to a variable, the variable’s type must be a supertype of (or the same as) the type of the incoming object.

It is important to emphasize the distinction between the type of the variable and the type of the object. The variable myShape ‘looks’ like a Shape, but actually holds a Rectangle.

In this sense, the type of the variable defines an interface. When you interact with myShape, you interact with the Rectangle, but you only do so in Shape-specific ways.

Type of the Object

To show that myShape actually contains a Rectangle, consider this implementation of Shape:

and this implementation of Rectangle:

If you run myShape.description(), you would get the following result:

because the underlying object is of type Rectangle. The references in shape are references to Rectangle methods.

Type of the Variable

To show that you can only interact with myShape in Shape-specific ways, assume that Rectangle also defines the following function:

If you run myShape.describeRectangularProperties(), you would get the following compile-time error:

because the variable myShape is of type Shape, and therefore cannot expose the Rectangle-specific method describeRectangularProperties().

Type Parameters

When talking about Collections, Shape and Rectangle would show up as type parameters (as in List<Shape>and List<Rectangle>). Classes like these, which depend on type parameters, are called Generics.

The role of Shape and Rectangle as type parameters is a bit more involved. Before diving into collections, let’s consider a more general generic:

Although it may seem natural, you can’t assign a Generic<Rectangle> object to a Generic<Shape> variable. In other words, this might be invalid:

That is because objects of type Generic<Shape>/Generic<Rectangle> don’t just encapsulate Shape/Rectangle objects. They also encapsulate methods whose behavior depends on the supplied type parameter (Shape or Rectangle). And that complicates things.

So, let’s break this down. In methods, type parameters can show up in only two places:

Return Type

In this Drawable interface:

…the type parameter T only shows up in the return type of the encapsulated abstract methods.

In Kotlin, such type parameters are marked by putting the out keyword before the type parameter in the Generic’s definition.

Argument Type

In this Stackable interface:

…the type parameter T only shows up as an argument type of the encapsulated abstract methods.

In Kotlin, such type parameters are marked by putting the in keyword before the type parameter in the Generic’s definition.

Covariance

Consider an immutable collection like List<Shape>. Once it is constructed, the only thing you can do is to read from it — therefore, its internal methods will only return Shapes, never ingest them. This is similar to the Drawable interface from above.

Such generics have a very special property — they follow the same inheritance relations as their type parameters:

If you think about it, this makes sense — anywhere we require an object that returns Shape, we can send an object that returns Rectangles. The important words here being “returns”.

This property is called “covariance” because the generics’ type hierarchies co-vary with the type parameters’ hierarchies.

The Need for Immutable Collections

Covariance would be a very useful property for collections: it feels natural and it makes code more intuitive. But it is only possible with immutable collections.

You see, mutable collections need to expose methods for adding and removing elements; these methods would have to accept the type parameter as an argument. As discussed above, that means the mutable collections can’t be covariant.

To make this last paragraph clearer, let’s look at an example. If we allow mutable collections to be covariant, the following code would be valid:

But let’s see what can go wrong if we allow it:

The last line would throw a runtime error! This is because the last line is trying to add a Circle to a MutableList<Rectangle>.

There are two ways the above error could have been avoided:

  1. If rectanglesList couldn’t be put into a variable with type MutableList<Shape> in the first place (i.e., no covariance)
  2. If shapesList and rectanglesList didn’t have methods like add() (i.e., no mutability)

Even if type-checks were added to all the write-methods in the Mutable Collections, those type checks would produce their own runtime errors/exceptions…which goes against the Kotlin philosophy of having as much compile-time type safety as possible.

The take-home message here is:

Mutability and covariance cannot be achieved in the same Collections interface.

Conclusion

  1. Mutable collections can be read from and written to. But Kotlin strives to avoid all runtime failures, therefore, these mutable collections are invariant.
  2. Immutable collections are covariant, but they’re…well…immutable. Still, Kotlin does provide mechanisms for doing useful things with these immutable collections (like filtering values or creating new immutable collections from existing ones). This article gives a nice list of examples:

Read-only collections in Kotlin, leads to better coding.

Use mutable collections while building your collection from elements.

Eventually though, transfer them to immutable collections, which will give you the added benefit of covariant assignments whenever needed.

Click 👏 to say “thanks!” and help others find this article.

entry.title: Setting up Your Workflow for Competitive Programming in Kotlin

link.title: Setting up Your Workflow for Competitive Programming in Kotlin

entry.content:
Get started in a matter of minutes!

This is a follow-up to my previous article, where I convince you to try Kotlin for Competitive Programming. But if you’re already convinced, then this article is for you! It is a step-by-step guide for setting up your local environment.

What we are aiming for

Your local workflow should help you achieve a few different things:

  1. A consistent process for starting a new contest, and for creating new solution files.
  2. Quick access to repetitive code that is necessary for reading input and writing output in every problem
  3. Access to tools like the Intellisense, a Read-Eval-Print Loop (REPL), and a debugging interface.

The following setup ensures all of these things for you.

Setup: Step-by-Step Guide

Step 1

Download and install IntelliJ IDEA (Community Edition will do) on your system.

Step 2

Download the latest version of the kotlin-cp.zip file from this GitHub Releases page.

Step 3

Launch the IDE, and go to File -> Import Settings.

Import the settings file you downloaded in Step 2.

Click OK.

Restart Intellij IDEA.

Usage: Step-by-Step Guide

Let’s say you want to participate in this CodeForces contest (CodeForces Global Round 8).

Let’s walk through the typical workflow:

Step 1 — Creating a New Project for the Contest

Start by creating an appropriately named Kotlin project:

Step 2 — Creating a New File for a Problem

Now, let’s say you want to solve the first problem in the contest:

Create a new file to start writing up the solution. First select the src folder in the Project navigation pane:

Then press alt + N to create a new solution file (this shortcut comes from the settings you imported from the kotlin-cp.zip file earlier). Name the new file based on the problem title:

Digression: Understanding the Template (Skip if you Want)

Before you start coding up the solution, you’ll have to understand the template. You can see the full source code for the template here. It is based on the template in this blog post (by Spheniscine, on CodeForces).

At the top, you have a set of convenience functions for parsing console input:

The functions are all declared private, because each solution file must be self-contained. When you create a new file for the next problem, it will declare the same set of functions, but they will be private only to that file, just like these are private only to this file.

These input parsing functions are used in main:

The actual code to solve each test case is written in the solveTestCase() function of the solution class. Note that the name of the class is the same as the name of the file you provided earlier:

This class is declared private, in case there is a need to use the input parsing functions inside of it.

Okay, now back to the steps.

Step 3: Parsing the Console Input

Note that the first line of the main function takes care of reading the number of test cases and looping over them:

You only have to write the code to parse the individual test cases:

And provide the parsed input to the solveTestCase() function call:

Notice that an error shows up as soon as you provide the inputs to solveTestCase(). That’s because you haven’t written the definition of the function yet. It’s part of the next step.

Step 4 — Writing the Code to Solve the Problem

First things first, you need to change the function signature to match the call in the main function. This can be done from the ‘error bulb’ drop-down:

This will add the appropriate input arguments to the function solveTestCase():

Then change the output type for the function, and write out your solution:

Digression: Helpful Tools

If you want to run the code while providing input from the console, press Ctrl + Shift + F10:

If you want to debug the code, put in a break-point in the left gutter next to the line from where you want to start debugging, and press Shift + F9:

If you want to open the Kotlin REPL to quickly try out some code, you can do that by pressing Alt + K (this shortcut was added in the settings in the kotlin-cp.zip file):

Step 5 — Submit Your Solution

Since the code in the file is self-contained, submitting is easy.

On some websites, you would copy-paste the whole file contents into an editor. In CodeForces, you need to upload the file:

Conclusion

And that’s it!

It may seem long because I’ve tried to be as explicit as possible about all things you need to do. But follow these steps one or two times, and soon you’ll be doing it all of this in a matter of seconds.

Oh, and do take the time to get familiar with the debugger (Shift + F9) and the Kotlin REPL (Alt + K) later on — they are very helpful in practice.

Happy coding!

entry.title: Kotlin for Competitive Programming
entry.content:
The new language of choice

I started using Kotlin for competitive programming a few months back. I’m finally able to enjoy the process of solving problems without getting lost in the syntax or the setup. I’m writing this article hoping to inspire you to try Kotlin for competitive programming too.

If you are inspired already, you should check out this article instead:

Setting up Your Workflow for Competitive Programming in Kotlin

The JetBrains folks do have a page discussing Kotlin for Competitive Programming; but I feel like the content on that page is slightly advanced, especially for people who are just starting out. Hopefully, this article can serve as a gentler introduction.

I’ve broken this article into two sections:

  1. In the first, I’ll share some example solutions that I have written in Kotlin. I have chosen these examples to cover a few different Kotlin features that I find very useful.
  2. In the second, I’ll discuss in detail how Kotlin compares to other popular languages used in Competitive Programming.

Examples

Let’s dive right in!

Example 1: Kids With the Greatest Number of Candies

In case you need to refer to the original problem statement, here is the link:

Kids With the Greatest Number of Candies - LeetCode

The input for each test case is:

  1. An array of integers denoting the number of candies each kid has
  2. An integer denoting the number of extra candies.

The problem boils down to this: for each kid, you need to determine if giving the kid all of the extra candies will make him/her have the greatest number of candies in the group. We need to output an array of booleans expressing this. The function signature is:

fun kidsWithCandies(candies: IntArray, extraCandies: Int): BooleanArray

In Kotlin, we can solve this in two lines:

fun kidsWithCandies(candies: IntArray, extraCandies: Int): BooleanArray {
    val maxCandies = candies.max()

    return BooleanArray(
        candies.size,
        { index -> candies[index] + extraCandies >= maxCandies!! }
    )
}

The last line is where all the magic happens:

return BooleanArray(
    candies.size,
    { index -> candies[index] + extraCandies >= maxCandies!! }
)

In it, we are constructing and returning a BooleanArray. The signature for the BooleanArray constructor is this:

BooleanArray(size: Int, init: (Int) -> Boolean)

The first argument to the constructor is the size of the array — candies.size in this case. The second argument is an init function, with the type (Int) -> Boolean — it takes in an Int (the index), and outputs a Boolean (the value to fill in at that index). We can encapsulate absolutely any initialization logic we want in this second argument.

Notice how convenient this is…Kotlin gives us a way to elegantly construct and initialize any array with just one line of code!

To further simplify this, there are two syntactic rules of Kotlin that we can make use of:

Passing trailing lambdas — “…if the last parameter of a function is a function, then a lambda expression passed as the corresponding argument can be placed outside the parentheses.”

So, we can simplify to this:

return BooleanArray(candies.size) { index ->
    candies[index] + extraCandies >= maxCandies!!
}
Implicit name of single parameter — “It’s very common that a lambda expression has only one parameter…The parameter will be implicitly declared under the name it"

So, we can simplify further to this:

return BooleanArray(candies.size) {
    candies[it] + extraCandies >= maxCandies!!
}

This is the final code. Take a few seconds to understand and internalize the syntax.

fun kidsWithCandies(candies: IntArray, extraCandies: Int): BooleanArray {
    val maxCandies = candies.max()

    return BooleanArray(candies.size) {
        candies[it] + extraCandies >= maxCandies!!
    }
}

Example 2: Chef and Price Control

Here is the link to the problem:

Contest Page | CodeChef

The input is:

  1. An array of integers denoting the original selling prices for a set of goods
  2. An integer denoting a new price ceiling that must be applied to all the goods.

We need to compute the total loss due to the introduction of the price ceiling. The problem boils down to this: for each good, if the ceiling is lower than the original price, we need to calculate the difference between the original price and the price ceiling, then output the sum of these values:

fun solve(prices: IntArray, priceCeiling: Int): Int

This is the one-line solution:

fun solve(prices: IntArray, priceCeiling: Int): Int {
    return prices.fold(0) { agg, e ->
        agg + (e- minOf(priceCeiling, e))
    }
}

The fold function allows you to aggregate the values in an array; fold iterates through the array, and applies the provided function to the aggregated value agg, and the next element e. The first argument to fold is what the aggregated value is initialized with— in this case, 0.

As you can see, this elegantly solves the problem in one line. Start with an aggregated value of 0, then keep adding e-minOf(priceCeiling,e) to the aggregated value. If the price ceiling did not cause the price of the good to fall, that expression will be 0, otherwise, it will be equal to the incurred loss for that good.

Example 3: Middle of the Linked List

Null values play an important role in many data structures. For example, in a Binary Tree, when a node has no left/right child, the value of the left/right attribute of the node is set to null. Similarly, you know you have reached the last node of a Linked List, when the next node is a null value.

Sometimes people have the perception that there are no nulls in Kotlin. But this is not true. Kotlin only requires you to be explicit about the nulls in your program. The official Kotlin documentation on Null Safety states:

Kotlin’s type system is aimed at eliminating the danger of null references from code

Whenever you assign a variable to a possibly null expression, the variable’s type must be nullable:

>>> val x = 3
>>> var y: Int = if (x>2) x else null
error: null can not be a value of a non-null type Int
>>> var y: Int? = if (x>2) x else null
>>> print(y)
3

Here, Int? is the nullable version of Int.

There are also ways to remove null values from your program. One such way is using the elvis operator, denoted by ?::

>>> var z: Int = y ?: 0
>>> print(z)
3

Note that despite y being of nullable type Int?, z is of type Int. As explained in the docs:

Elvis Operator — “If the expression to the left of ?: is not null, the elvis operator returns it, otherwise it returns the expression to the right. Note that the right-hand side expression is evaluated only if the left-hand side is null.”

In fact, the right side of the ?: doesn’t have to be an expression, and you don’t have to assign to a variable either:

>>> y ?: print("y is null")
3
>>> y = null
>>> y ?: print("y is null")
y is null

Armed with that basic understanding, let’s take a look at this last example problem:

Middle of the Linked List - LeetCode

We need to return the middle node of a singly Linked List given the head. We are also given this starter code:

class ListNode(var value: Int) {
    var next: ListNode? = null
}

The next property has a nullable type. This is because for the last node, next would have to be null.

We will solve this problem using the two pointer method. One pointer will iterate through the list twice as fast as the other. When the faster pointer reaches the end of the list, the slower pointer will be in the middle.

We’ll initialize the slow pointer at the first node and the fast one at the second:

fun middleNode(head: ListNode?): ListNode? {
    var slow = head
    var fast = head?.next ?: return head
    // TODO...
}

We have to do a 'safe call’ with head?.next instead of just head.next because head could be null (it is of nullable type); but don’t worry about that too much — Intellisense will tell you to make that change automatically. The important thing to notice is how we are using the elvis operator. In case there is no node after head, we know we have a Linked List of size one, and we can just return head.

For all other non-corner cases, we have the while loop:

fun middleNode(head: ListNode?): ListNode? {
    var slow = head
    var fast = head?.next ?: return head
    while(true) {
        slow = slow?.next
        fast = fast.next?.next ?: return slow
    }
}

We move the fast pointer two nodes ahead and the slow pointer one node ahead every time. If the fast pointer ever becomes null, that means it has reached the end of the Linked List and we can return the middle node.

Take a minute to understand and internalize the above syntax.

Kotlin vs Other Languages

Now that we’ve seen some examples, let’s have a more in-depth discussion of how Kotlin compares with other languages commonly used in Competitive Programming.

Kotlin vs Java

Kotlin is essentially an improvement of Java. It runs on the JVM just like Java, but it extends many Java classes — especially the Java Collections library — and it removes the need for a lot of boilerplate code.

Consider the Java ArrayList<Integer>, for example. Every time you want to add an int to the ArrayList, you first have to convert it to an Integer object. This is especially frustrating when you are in the middle of a contest.

Kotlin on the other hand has a very easy-to-use arrays system. There is an in-built class for each primitive-type array, as well as a parameterized Array<T> type, and they all come fully loaded with convenience and extension functions, as we have seen in the examples.

For a more exhaustive comparison, you can refer to this page from the official website.

Kotlin vs Python

We all know the fundamental problem with using Python for Competitive Programming — it is very slow. Because it is not compiled down to an executable, it is run line-by-line (this is what people mean when they say Python is an ‘interpreted’ language). This causes a very large performance overhead. Kotlin code is compiled and run in the JVM, so it is much faster.

But we don’t use Python because it is fast; we use it because it is easy to write. “It’s basically English!” we say. Well, I hope the examples have convinces you that Kotlin syntax is quite intuitive and English-like too. More importantly, Kotlin manages to do so while being type-safe (unlike Python, where you’ll often find yourself scratching your head wondering if the function you wrote took in a list or a tuple as an argument).

Kotlin vs C++

I know C++ has evolved a lot in recent years, and the syntax has become a lot more expressive. Despite that, I would advocate that Kotlin has at least two clear advantages that over C++:

  1. The functional syntax of Kotlin is exceptionally elegant. From what I’ve found on the web, it is far superior to that of C++.
  2. Kotlin has an REPL (like the Python console)! You can use it to quickly test out snippets of code. In C++, this is simply not possible without creating an executable or starting a debugger.

Kotlin vs C++: Performance

It is safe to say that if you are looking for raw speed, there is no better option than C++ right now. Once you’ve surmounted the initial learning curve and are vying for the top few spots in contests, you’ll have to switch to C++.

The main reason C++ is so fast is that it compiles down to an executable that is ‘native’ to the system. So if your online judge is running your C++ code on a Linux server, that code gets compiled and then run by Linux itself (this is why Windows and Linux come with different C++ compilers — MSVC and g++, respectively). Kotlin on the other hand, compiles the code down to the level of a JVM (which run on top of the OS). JVMs introduce abstractions to make it possible for the same Java code to run on any OS; unfortunately for us, these abstractions cause performance overhead.

But this could change in the future. There are a set of ‘Kotlin/Native’ compilers that compile Kotlin code down to an OS executable. Currently, Kotlin/Native compilers exist for Windows, Mac and Linux! Unfortunately, almost all online judges run Kotlin code in the JVM. Should this change in the future though, Kotlin will become truly comparable to C++ for competitive programming…even for the pros!

Conclusion

I hope this article has gotten you pumped to start competitive programming in Kotlin. To get started right away, I suggest you go through this article:

Setting up Your Workflow for Competitive Programming in Kotlin

entry.title: A Zero-Math Intuitive Understanding of the ROC-AUC Metric

link.title: A Zero-Math Intuitive Understanding of the ROC-AUC Metric

entry.content:
No math or formulas. Yes images and animations.

Understanding the Axes

This is what a typical ROC graph looks like:

Before we get into anything else, we need to understand what the axes mean. Without getting into confusing formulas, here’s the simplest possible explanation:

  1. The x-axis (False Positive Rate, or FPR), is the fraction of actually negative examples the model is tagging as positive (False Positive).
  2. The y-axis (True Positive Rate, or TPR), is the fraction of actually positive examples the model is tagging as positive (True Positive).

Notice the parallelism between both! Essentially, the ROC curve is a True Positive vs False Positive curve, with both axes normalized.

Relation to Thresholds

Whenever we see a line graph, we tend to think in terms of a linear progression through time, or some parameter represented on the x-axis. As we increase the parameter on the x-axis, the line graph progresses. The thought process is usually this: “for a given value on the x-axis, the graph gives me the corresponding value on the y-axis”.

But the ROC is subtle in that way — it isn’t a mapping from FPR values (x-axis) to TPR values (y-axis), because you can’t really calculate the TPR as a function of FPR. So what is varying as the ROC curve moves away from the origin? The answer is (drum roll, please): the threshold.

If we dig deeper into most classification models, we see that they don’t just assign a label to a data point, they assign a score to a data point, and then compare that score against a threshold to decide whether to classify it as positive or negative:

So, given a threshold, the model will produce a classification for every data point. And for a given set of classifications, you’ll get one value each for TPR and FPR. But, as you vary the threshold, TPR and FPR will both vary between 0 to 1. That is why we say the threshold varies as the ROC curve progresses.

Extreme Cases

To visualize this properly, let’s begin by considering the extreme cases; this will give us a better vantage point for understanding how the ROC curve works in the other cases.

First, consider the case when the threshold is set to a maximum value. Nothing gets scored higher than the threshold, and nothing gets tagged as positive by the model. This is when the ROC curve is at (0,0):

Now consider the other extreme case — when the threshold is at its minimum. Everything gets scored higher than the threshold, and everything gets tagged as positive by the model. This is when the ROC curve is at (1,1):

Everything In-Between

Running through everything between those two extremes looks like this:

As the model threshold decreases, the total number of positive predictions will increase. The ROC graph expresses how those positive predictions get divided up between True Positives and False Positives.

Desirable Characteristics of the ROC Curve

Now that we know what the ROC curve represents, we can start understanding what would make a given ROC curve ‘good’ or ‘bad’.

Let’s take a look at the axes again:

It’s pretty obvious that we want True Positives and we don’t want False Positives. In terms of the axes, we want to move up the y-axis, but we don’t want to move forward on the x-axis. However, the ROC curve goes all the way from (0,0) to (1,1)…in other words, you’re gonna move all the way across the x-axis, no matter what.

Therefore, the quality of an ROC curve must have something to do with the shape of the curve. To understand what shape would be considered good, we go back to the threshold picture to try to understand what makes a classification model better. Clearly, a model that scores the data points like this:

is worse than one that scores its data points like this:

which is worse than one that scores it data points like this (ideal case):

If we compare all of these along with their ROC curves, a clear pattern begins to emerge:

If more white points (actually positive data points) rank higher than black points (actually negative points), the ROC curve rises up the y-axis (TPR) before it moves forward on the x-axis (FPR). And the earlier the TPR rises, the larger the area under the curve is:

And that’s why you will often see the metric ROC-AUC (ROC-Area Under Curve) or AUROC (Area Under ROC) being used as a measure of the performance of the classification algorithm.

Essentially, a better ROC curve is one with a larger area under the curve, because that implies that more positive examples are ranked higher than negative examples by the classification model, i.e., the model has a better separation of positive and negative data points (in the right direction).

Conclusion

Hopefully, these animations and these explanations have given you a more intuitive understanding of what the ROC curve is and why we choose the Area Under the ROC curve as a metric for a classification algorithm’s performance.

entry.title: PyTest: An Introduction to Parametrization
entry.content:
One Trick for Phenomenally Smaller Unit Tests

A guide to writing *very* concise unit tests for your Python package.

The first section will explain the structure of the accompanying package and how to set it up on your system. If you just want to see examples of parametrization in PyTest, you can skip straight over to the second section, “Parametrizing Tests”.

To clone the source code accompanying this article, click here.

Package Structure and Setup

The cloned repository will contain a package called efficient_dedup and a tests folder containing test cases.

The package is designed to perform efficient deduplication (remove duplicate values) in Python lists. It does this in two steps — first, it sorts the list, then it uses one of the deduplication algorithms to deduplicate the sorted list. Note that this package is just illustrative; as such, a lot of the code is functionally redundant. This is the package structure:

efficient_dedup
|
| - efficient_deduplication
| - deduplication_algorithms
| - sorting_algorithms
|
| - tests
    |
    | - test_efficient_deduplication

It is based on the Strategy Design Pattern. The EfficientDeduplicator class defined in the efficient_deduplication module is the context:

requiring a strategy implementation from each of the deduplication_algorithms and sorting_algorithms modules.

There are only two strategy behaviors defined in the sorting_algorithms module, and they are both encapsulated in a single class, SortingAlgorithm; the specific behavior you want can be chosen by setting the reverse argument to True or False:

The deduplication_algorithms module contains four different implementations, each encapsulated in a different class. The first class, DeduplicationAlgorithm, acts as the base class for the other three implementations (this is not the actual code, as definitions of the functions have been omitted here):

To run the test cases, cd into the root folder of the package and run the following command:

> cd <git-repo-root>/efficient_dedup
> python -m pytest

Parametrizing Tests

So, let’s summarize before proceeding. We have a context class called EfficientDeduplicator, which requires two strategies: a SortingAlgorithm and a DeduplicationAlgorithm. This context class has only one function, deduplicate_efficiently.

We would like to test deduplicate_efficiently with all possible combinations of the strategies, and on a few different test data. As we will see, it is possible to do all that in just one test case, if we make use of parametrization.

Parametrizing Over Data

This is the most basic test case we can write:

Let’s say we want to perform this test with a few different possible inputs, i.e., a few different values for the variable list_with_duplicates. First, we make list_with_duplicates an argument in the test function. Then, we provide a list of values for that argument through the @pytest.marker.parametrize decorator.

This is the general procedure for doing parametrization in Pytest:

  1. You specify the variable you want to parametrize over in the arguments list of the test function
  2. Then you use the @pytest.marker.parametrize decorator to provide a list of values for the variable.

Parametrizing over Classes

Now, let’s say we wanted to run the basic test with all possible different implementations of the DeduplicationAlgorithm, but keep the data the same. This can be achieved using a clever combination of Pytest parametrization, Python’s inspect module, and the fact that classes are first-class citizens in Python (meaning they can be passed around as arguments to functions).

To get a list of all the classes in the deduplication_algorithms module, we can import the module, and then run the following code:

print([
    getattr(deduplication_algorithms, name)
    for name, obj
    in inspect.getmembers(deduplication_algorithms)
    if inspect.isclass(obj)
])

which gives us a list of the classes in the module:

[
<class 'efficient_dedup.deduplication_algorithms.DeduplicationAlgorithm'>, 
<class 'efficient_dedup.deduplication_algorithms.HashSetDeduplicationAlgori
thm'>,
<class 'efficient_dedup.deduplication_algorithms.CustomComparisonDeduplicationAlgorithm'>,
<class 'efficient_dedup.deduplication_algorithms.LookaheadCustomComparisonDeduplicationAlgorithm'>
]

which we can then pass into the @pytest.marker.parametrize decorator:

et voila. You have achieved class parametrization in Pytest!

Combining Data and Class Parametrization

A great feature of Pytest is that if you stack many @pytest.marker.parametrize decorators on a test function, it automatically runs the test for all possible combinations across all the decorators (like a set product). We’ll conclude by using this feature to combine both the above parametrizations in a single test case; in fact, we’ll also throw in a parametrization over the reverse property of the SortingAlgorithm :

This is the final form of the test case in the package you would have cloned. If you run Pytest verbosely:

> python -m pytest -v

you’ll observe outputs like this:

tests/test_efficient_deduplication.py::TestEfficientDeduplicators::test_deduplicate_efficiently
[DeduplicationAlgorithm-True-list_with_duplicates0] 
PASSED [33%]

The second line in the above output lists the exact combination of parameters used in the test case.

Conclusion

Use the techniques described in this article to write more concise and effective Python test cases in the future!
